plain_title: Distress when your body or life doesn't match who you are
one_liner: Lasting distress because your gender identity doesn't match the sex you were assigned at birth.
in_simple_words: Gender dysphoria is the distress some transgender and gender-diverse people feel when their inner sense of gender doesn't match their body or the sex recorded at birth, and the way others treat them because of it. Being transgender is not a disorder. The diagnosis describes the distress, and exists mainly so people can get care. Not every trans person has dysphoria, and the distress usually eases when a person can live as themselves with support and, when wanted, medical care.
what_it_can_feel_like: Puberty felt like my body was betraying me in front of everyone. When I could finally say the word 'trans', the fog started to lift.
The dysphoria was never about hating myself. It was about being seen as someone I wasn't, every single day.
My mum didn't understand at first. She went to a parents' group. Now she corrects people before I do.
common_signs: A strong, lasting sense that your gender differs from your assigned sex
Distress about your body's sex characteristics, or dread about puberty changes
A strong wish to be treated and seen as your gender
Distress or difficulty in daily life because of this
Lasting at least six months (DSM wording), though many people feel it far longer

myths_vs_facts.myth: Being transgender is a mental illness.
myths_vs_facts.fact: It isn't. The World Health Organization moved gender incongruence out of its mental disorders chapter in ICD-11. The DSM diagnosis describes distress, which can be relieved, not identity, which is not a problem.

myths_vs_facts.myth: It's a phase, especially in teenagers.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Questioning is normal and some young people's feelings change, which is why care is careful and staged. For many, the identity is stable and lifelong, and being dismissed causes real harm.

myths_vs_facts.myth: Support and affirmation make it worse.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Research consistently links family acceptance and respectful care with lower depression and suicide risk. Rejection and 'conversion' efforts are linked with worse outcomes and are condemned by major medical bodies.

how_common.plain: Around 1 in 200 US adults and about 1 in 70 US teenagers identify as transgender. Not all have dysphoria, and far fewer have the formal diagnosis.
how_common.figure: About 0.5% of US adults and 1.4% of youth aged 13–17 identify as transgender (Williams Institute, 2022)

what_helps.plain_summary: Care is individual and should be led by the person. Many people are helped most by social support: using their name and pronouns, changing how they dress or present, and being accepted at home and school. Mental health support helps with distress, anxiety, or depression, and is not aimed at changing identity. Some people choose medical options, such as puberty-pausing or hormone treatment or, in adulthood, surgery, after assessment by specialist teams following international standards such as WPATH's, with all medication prescribed and monitored by a doctor. Access and rules differ a lot between countries, and for under-18s they're changing in several places.
evidence_based_options: Social support and affirmation at home, school, and work
Mental health support for distress, depression, or anxiety, not aimed at changing identity
Specialist gender services for assessment and, where chosen, medical care under international standards
Family support programmes and peer support
self_help_that_supports_care: Finding peer community, online or local, run by trusted organisations
Small changes that ease dysphoria day to day: clothing, hair, name
Knowing your rights at school and work
Looking after mental health; dysphoria is tougher when you're isolated

when_to_reach_out: If distress about your gender is making life hard, talk to someone you trust, a doctor, or an LGBTQ+ support line. If you're a parent, your acceptance is the single most protective thing you can offer; parent helplines and groups can help you get there. If you're thinking about ending your life, please use the crisis strip now; the lines listed there understand trans experience.
is_not: Not fitting gender stereotypes, being gender non-conforming, or being gay, lesbian, or bisexual isn't gender dysphoria. Being transgender without distress isn't a diagnosis. Questioning is not a disorder.
hope_note: People who are supported to live as themselves describe relief, ease, and ordinary joy. Dysphoria lifts; the person stays.

content_notes: Suicide risk statistics for trans youth are deliberately kept off the card face to avoid harm; the crisis strip carries the lines instead.

language_convention_note: 'Transgender person', 'trans person', and 'gender-diverse person' are the terms communities use; 'person with gender dysphoria' is used only for the diagnosis itself.
in_young_people: Dysphoria often becomes intense at puberty. Care for under-18s is staged: social support first, then specialist assessment, with medical options only through specialist teams and, in many countries, strict rules. Family acceptance is the strongest protective factor for a young person's mental health.
across_cultures: Many cultures recognise genders beyond two, including hijra in South Asia, two-spirit people in some Native American nations, and fa'afafine in Samoa. Laws, safety, and access to care vary enormously by country, and migration and family expectations shape what support looks like.
